paras: The lynching of George Parrott, known as "Big Nose George", took place on the night of March 22, 1881, in Rawlins, Wyoming Territory, when a party of men took him from the county jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Parrott was already under sentence of death for murder, and the hanging followed his attack on the jailer in an escape attempt earlier that evening. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and the Cheyenne Daily Leader called it "the sensation of the territory."

Newspapers described Parrott as a road agent and one of the "Elk Mountain murderers," a gang said to have tried to wreck a Union Pacific train near Medicine Bow and to have killed deputy sheriffs Tip Vincent and Widdowfield. According to the Morris Tribune, he was captured months later, confessed, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to hang on April 2, though one wire version gave April 24 and another April 26.

At 7:30 on the evening of March 22, Jailor Robert Rankin entered the jail corridor to lock up the prisoners and was struck over the head by Parrott, who had removed his heavy shackles during the afternoon. Mrs. Rankin locked the outer door, a sister of the jailer ran to raise the alarm, and a crowd hurried to the jail, secured the prisoners and released the injured jailer. The Leader's Rawlins correspondent reported that extra guards were posted and that threats of lynching were being made in the town.

At about 10:55 that night, according to the Leader's second special, a party of masked men took Parrott out of the jail to a telegraph pole opposite the railroad machine shops. The Juniata Sentinel's fuller account said the men rode into town and overpowered Sheriff Rankin and his deputies, while the Morris Tribune and a Rawlins telegram printed in the Jamestown Alert described "citizens of Rawlins" who gathered at the jail and led him to a pole near the depot. He was first stood on a barrel that was kicked away, which only choked him, and was then made to climb a ladder with the rope around his neck. His reported last words were "I will jump off, boys, and break my neck"; the fall did not break his neck, and he freed his hands, climbed the pole, begged to be shot, and died after several minutes.

The Morris Tribune said the lynching was "quietly conducted" and that the coroner cut down the body and took charge of it. No report of an inquest verdict, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage. In July the Leader reported that Mrs. Rankin had been given a gold watch for preventing the escape. In August the French Consul General in New York asked the territorial governor for a death certificate for "George Parrot, alias George Au-Gros-Nez," on behalf of his widow, saying he had been "lynched" at Rawlins.

Coverage came entirely from the white press, beginning with the Cheyenne Daily Leader's two specials from Rawlins, which were relayed by wire to papers from Sacramento to Washington on March 23 and 24. Headlines stressed the mob and the drama, such as the Evening Star's "Hanged by a Mob," the Wheeling Register's "Comes to His End at the Hands of a Mob," and the Memphis Appeal's "Short Shrift for a Desperado." Weekly digests later reduced the story to a line about a "famous Wyoming stage robber and desperado," some dating it to the night of the 23d and one naming the victim "George F. Warden."

The Juniata Sentinel called the lynchers "the masked deputies of Judge Lynch" and ended that "the Elk Mountain murder was avenged," while the Louisiana Capitolian called it a "dramatic incident" of Far-Western life in which Judge Lynch "shortened his sentence by a few days." No paper in the coverage mentions the race of Parrott or of the men who hanged him.

Accounts differ on who did the hanging: the Leader and the Juniata Sentinel describe masked men, the latter riding in from outside town, while the Morris Tribune and the Jamestown Alert's telegram describe townspeople gathering openly at the jail.

bases: A party of masked men, or by other accounts a gathering of citizens, took a condemned prisoner from the Rawlins jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A2, A13, A16).

Parrott, under sentence of death for murder, was taken from jail and hanged without legal authority by a 'party of masked men' or assembled 'citizens' (A2, A13, A16, A18); papers framed it as Judge Lynch anticipating the gallows after his escape attempt (A13, A22).

The Cheyenne Leader's Rawlins special (A2) is joined by separately worded accounts in the Juniata Sentinel (A13), the Morris Tribune and Jamestown Alert telegram (A16, A18), and the French consul's later letter (A24).

framing.detail: Eastern dailies ran the Cheyenne wire under headlines such as '"Big Nose" George Lynched' and 'Hanged by a Mob', quoting his last words.
The Juniata Sentinel called the lynchers 'the masked deputies of Judge Lynch' and closed that 'the Elk Mountain murder was avenged'.

The Louisiana Capitolian treated it as a 'dramatic incident' of the Far West in which Judge Lynch 'shortened his sentence by a few days'; the Memphis Appeal headlined it 'Short Shrift for a Desperado'.
